NV26-2's flagged contamination is a low-cost lesson for the
sampling plan above, not just a data-quality footnote: future
Giggenbach-bottle gas sampling at this terrace should avoid breaking
through fresh pavement and should re-check bottle seals in the field
before leaving the site.

**Water and gas geothermometers side by side.** Putting the gas
geothermometer estimates next to this project's existing water
geothermometers (Na/K-Giggenbach, Na/K-Fournier, quartz, chalcedony; 132
method/sample estimates across 63 thermal samples with complete
chemistry) against measured temperature, shown in @fig-geothermwatergas,
makes the pattern explicit rather than described only in prose: every
method except quartz and chalcedony over-predicts measured temperature, and
the one co-located point (NV26-1 gas / SBF_0001 water) sits
consistently with that pattern rather than as an outlier: the gas estimate
(228 degrees Celsius) lands closest to the Na/K estimates (153-173 degrees
Celsius) among the water methods, not the quartz/chalcedony pair (92-118
degrees Celsius), suggesting both the gas and the Na/K-based water
signatures are responding to a similar, deeper and hotter part of the
system than the silica-based estimates.

**A first PHREEQC test using the gas data.** The gas isotope and
conservative-ratio data collected here are also a natural input to the
PHREEQC gas-phase modeling already described in the Background section,
for the first time a test was possible rather than only a synthetic
self-test: SBF_0001's measured water chemistry was re-equilibrated against a
PHREEQC gas phase seeded with NV26-1's air-corrected CO2-to-H2S proportions
(96.5 to 3.5 percent) at 1 atmosphere, modeled as an open system
continuously resupplied by the fissure. Shown in @fig-gasphase, the result
is a substantive shift: pH drops from the water's measured 8.3 to a
modeled 5.7, and calcite, aragonite, and dolomite all move from
supersaturated (as PHREEQC already finds for the
water alone) to undersaturated. Read this says the water as
sampled is not simply sitting in equilibrium with the vent gas as sampled:
either the two were not collected from truly the same fluid parcel, gas and
liquid separate before either is caught at the surface, or the
reservoir pressure (not the 1 atmosphere used here as a simplification)
changes the picture. Any of those is a useful constraint on how this
system's gas and water should eventually be modeled together, not a result
to over-interpret from one sample pair.

```{r fig-gasphase}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/gas_analysis/gas_phase_fischer_pairing_before_after.png",
  "SBF_0001 water chemistry before and after PHREEQC equilibration with a GAS_PHASE seeded from NV26-1's measured composition.",
  alt = "Bar chart comparing pH and three carbonate mineral saturation indices before and after equilibrating a water sample with a measured gas composition.",
  id = "fig-gasphase"
)
```

## The thermal layer and the database on one map

**Data and method.** The thermal map used here is a georeferenced layout export
of the 2025 survey (O. Callahan, NBMG, unpublished imagery), in NAD83 / UTM zone 11N
(EPSG:26911), 16,907 by 4,477 pixels at about 0.17 by 0.10 m. A semi-transparent
temperature layer lies over a hillshade, with analyst annotations (yellow ellipses
and 13.5 m circles, outlines) drawn into the pixels. Each pixel was matched to the
nearest color of the 7-44 degree Celsius ramp in the calibrated legend (the TIFF has
no legend of its own, so the same stretch is assumed), keeping pixels within a fixed
color distance of the ramp and excluding the annotation colors. The mask was closed
over about 0.5 m, because the layer is speckled at pixel scale, and polygonized into
a table of thermal areas in the project database. The ramp saturates at 44 degrees Celsius.

**How much surface is hot.** A pixel by pixel count gives 488 m^2^ at or above 30
degrees Celsius; the 67 polygons total 480 m^2^ (@tbl-thermalareas). Grouped by the source
each polygon marks (@tbl-thermalsources and @fig-thermalsources), the Lower Terrace channel
holds the most (161 m^2^, 34 percent), followed by the resort tanks, pipe and pavement
(109 m^2^, 23 percent), the fissure zone (99 m^2^, 21 percent) and the creek-corridor springs
and seeps (49 m^2^, 10 percent, spread over 17 small polygons along the creek). A 13 m^2^
streak at the end of the resort pipe line is uncertain, and the annotated 13.5 m circles
(34 m^2^) are ambiguous. The annotation ellipses are an analyst's judgment, not a verified
geothermal boundary, and a pixel at 30 degrees Celsius is not necessarily geothermal.

| Class | Polygons | Area at or above 30 C (m^2^) |
|---------------------------------|---------|------------------|
| Inside the 10 large ellipses (geothermal anomalies) | 29 | 321 |
| Resort infrastructure (tanks, pipe, pavement) | 12 | 109 |
| Inside the 13.5 m circles (ambiguous) | 10 | 34 |
| Outside every outline | 14 | 12 |
| Other small | 2 | 3 |

: Polygons at or above 30 degrees Celsius from the georeferenced thermal map, by class. {#tbl-thermalareas}

| Lower Terrace channel (northwest-southeast) | 5 | 161 | 34% | 40.2 |

**Alignment with mapped structure.** In @fig-map-fissure, about 35 percent of the hot area lies within 5 m
of a mapped fissure and 61 percent within 15 m; 42 percent lies within 15 m of a mapped
fault. The hot streak of the fissure zone lies 0.8-1.6 m from mapped Fissures 42, 43
and 44, and within 5-7 m of White's historical "closed fissure 25" and "spring 25s"
[@white1968c], so features White recorded in the 1960s are thermally active again
along the same traces. The streak follows the trend of the Low Terrace Fault, and the
resort tanks sit about 8 m from the same fault. That alignment is a hypothesis, since
fault traces carry digitizing uncertainty, but it would fit White's observation that
discharge from the spa wells affected springs on the low terrace [@collar1990thesis;
@sorey1992]. Only 7 of the 53 mapped fissure traces have 1 m^2^ or more at or above 30
degrees Celsius within 3 m; the layer name marks them as closed, and what "closed"
means has not been confirmed.

```{r fig-map-fissure}
  alt = "Map of the fissure zone: a hot streak along mapped fissures, with SBF_0001, SBF_0002, SBW_0003 and NV26-1 on it and historical spring names.",
  id = "fig-map-fissure",
  width = "80%"
)
```

**Checking our own points against the layer.** Overlaying the points showed that the
stored position of SBF_0001 was about 50 m from the hot streak although its logger read
up to 88 degrees Celsius, and that SBW_0003 (the capped eruption pipe) had only a
provisional position. Positions placed in ArcGIS on the imagery now replace them:
SBF_0001 (moved about 50 m), SBF_0002 (4 m), SBW_0003 (61 m), SBS_0002 (141 m) and
SBO_00006 (3 m, set to the same spring area). The four fumarole and pipe points and
the NV26-1 gas-sample position now fall within 0.2-3.4 m of a hot pixel and about 1 m
of Fissure 42, and SBS_0002 within 1.5 m. Loggers at SBS_0006, SBS_0001, SBW_0002 and
SBF_0002 were already within about 1-2 m of hot pixels and SBW_0001 within 4 m.
SBS_0003 sits where the surface shows no thermal anomaly, and SBS_0004, destroyed, is
off the thermal map. Seven of the project's points lie within 10 m of a White or Collar
feature and now carry nine such names as aliases, among them the SBF_0001 and SBF_0002 fumaroles
renamed 25ss" and "spring 25ss"), SBO_00017 and SBO_00018 (spring 45), SBO_00020
(spring 46), SBO_00015 (spring 44e) and SBO_00011 (spring 50n), now carry those names as
aliases; the matches rest on proximity, not on a field-confirmed identity.

**The resort's contribution.** The A009 logger sits 7 m from the bright tank pads, so
the pads are the resort tanks (@fig-map-resort). Resort infrastructure accounts for 109
m^2^ (23 percent) of the area at or above 30 degrees Celsius, and the tank-adjacent
patches hold about 205 m^2^ at or above 20 degrees Celsius, about half of it at or above
30. No continuous path at or above 20 degrees Celsius connects the tanks to the creek:
the long diagonal band beside them, probably a road, ditch or paved edge, reads 15-20
and the creek 13-15 degrees Celsius, so any discharge band is cooler than the threshold
and cannot be separated from pavement and water. The route of the discharge is therefore
not mapped, and a field walk of the overflow is planned.

```{r fig-map-resort}
  alt = "Map of the resort tank area showing bright tank pads with a pipe line, a diagonal warm band beside them, and a separate hot channel to the southwest.",
  id = "fig-map-resort",
  width = "80%"

```

The chloride budget bounds the resort's share. On 1 May 2026 the creek chloride fluxes
between SBRR and SBBV differ by 48.1 g/s, which at the 820 mg/L thermal end-member is a
thermal inflow of 58.65 L/s, and the resort tank sample of the same day carried 849 mg/L.
Any resort water that reaches the creek between the two stations is counted in that
inflow. The pumping rate is not known, so @tbl-resortshare gives the share for a range of
rates, including the historical spa-well rates: an average of 60 gpm and a peak of 155 gpm
in 1945-52 [@white1968c; @collar1990thesis], about 60 gpm at its peak in 1989
[@collar1990thesis; @sorey1992], and 30 gpm from the 1985 driller's test, which is a test
yield and not an operating rate.

| Resort discharge reaching the creek | Chloride flux (g/s) | Share of 58.65 L/s | Remainder (L/s) |
|-------------------------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| 0.5 L/s | 0.42 | 0.9% | 58.1 |
| 1.0 L/s | 0.85 | 1.8% | 57.6 |
| 1.9 L/s (30 gpm, 1985 test) | 1.61 | 3.3% | 56.7 |
| 3.8 L/s (60 gpm, historical average) | 3.21 | 6.7% | 54.7 |
| 5 L/s | 4.25 | 8.8% | 53.5 |
| 9.8 L/s (155 gpm, historical peak) | 8.30 | 17.3% | 48.5 |
| 10 L/s | 8.49 | 17.7% | 48.3 |
| 20 L/s | 16.98 | 35.3% | 38.0 |

: Share of the 1 May 2026 thermal inflow that would be resort water, by discharge rate (resort tank chloride 849 mg/L; thermal end-member 820 mg/L). {#tbl-resortshare}

The A009 record shows how the resort operates now. Over 95 complete days from April to
September 2026 the tank temperature follows a smooth daily cycle: it cools from midnight
to a sharp minimum near 09:00, warms through the day, and plateaus near 75.9 degrees
Celsius from about 18:00 to midnight (@fig-a009). Variability between 5-minute readings is
0.2-0.3 degrees Celsius at every hour, so there is no pump-pulse signature, and weekdays
and weekends differ little (daily range 2.4 versus 3.1 degrees Celsius; p = 0.11 to 0.44
across the measures tested). Weekends show the same daytime warming, so operation is
daily, not the weekday-only pattern Collar recorded in 1989 [@collar1990thesis]. Because
air temperature cannot reheat a 75 degree tank, the warming phase is read as hot inflow,
and the tank is warming or at its plateau about 58 percent of the day (about 14 hours).
That fraction is an inference from the heat balance, not a flow measurement; scaled by
the historical rates it would put the time-averaged resort share at roughly 2 to 10 percent
of the thermal inflow.

```{r fig-a009}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/a009_hourly_profile.png",
  "Mean temperature of the resort holding tank (logger A009) by hour of day, April to September 2026, for weekdays and weekends.",
  alt = "Line plot of tank temperature falling from midnight to a 9 AM minimum, rising through the day, flattening in the evening; weekday and weekend match.",
  id = "fig-a009",
  width = "60%"
)
```

**What the thermal estimate does to the chloride and heat budgets.** The thermal map and the chloride balance measure different things: the map says where heat reaches the surface and over how much ground, and the balance says how much thermal water the creek receives. They connect in three ways. First, attribution: area is not discharge. The resort tanks hold 23 percent of the hot area but would carry 2 to 18 percent of the chloride (@tbl-resortshare), because hot tank surfaces and pipes shed heat from a small volume of water, while diffuse inflow along the creek moves more water through cooler ground. The map therefore says which sources to measure, and where a source's flow is measured its share is subtracted from the 58.65 L/s and the rest is natural discharge. Second, heat: the 480 m^2^ of polygons loses an estimated 0.2-0.4 MW to the air (@tbl-heatbudget), against 11-28 MW carried above creek temperature by 58.65 L/s of water at 60-130 degrees Celsius, so surface hot ground is only about 1-3 percent of the heat. The heat budget is dominated by water leaving through the subsurface toward the creek, which the surface map cannot see and the chloride balance can. Third, a creek energy balance on 1 May 2026 (SBRR 15.2 degrees Celsius at 0.317 m^3^/s, SBBV 23.7 at 0.425) implies a total inflow of 108 L/s at about 49 degrees Celsius. If 58.65 L/s of that is thermal water and the rest is at 10-20 degrees Celsius, the thermal water entered at about 77 degrees Celsius (73-81), close to the 75 degree resort tank and the 65-72 degree terrace features. That is a consistency check on the chloride-based discharge and the end-member assumption, not a heat budget: it rests on one date and instantaneous thermometer readings and neglects heat lost to the air, so it is a lower bound.

| Quantity (columns follow the order of the values listed) | Low | Mid | High |
|----------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|
| Surface heat loss from polygons at or above 30 C, MW (convective coefficient 10, 15, 25 W/m^2^/K) | 0.23 | 0.30 | 0.44 |
| Heat carried above creek temperature by the thermal inflow, MW (thermal water at 60, 90, 130 C) | 10.98 | 18.34 | 28.15 |
| Surface loss as a share of the heat carried, % (60, 90, 130 C) | 2.7 | 1.6 | 1.1 |
| Implied temperature of the thermal inflow, C (non-thermal inflow at 10, 15.2, 20 C) | 81.1 | 76.8 | 72.8 |

: Order of magnitude heat estimates. Emissivity 0.95, ambient 10 C, creek water 15.2 C, thermal inflow 58.65 L/s. {#tbl-heatbudget}

**Is the resort still pumping on the same schedule?** By month, the A009 daily cycle persists with the same shape. The median hour of the daily minimum runs from about 09:30 in May and 09:25 in July to 09:00 in August and 08:15 in September, and the tank is warming or at its plateau for about half to two-thirds of the day in every month (0.48 to 0.65 of the hourly steps). From August to September the tank runs about 1 degree Celsius cooler (mean 75.4 to 74.8) with larger swings (daily range 2.6 to 3.0), which fits cooler nights or slightly less hot inflow, not a different schedule; the record cannot say which. @fig-resort-curve puts the pumping rate in context: at the historical average of 60 gpm the resort share is 6.7 percent if pumped continuously and 3.9 percent scaled by the 58 percent duty cycle.

Two limits apply. The July 2025 resort-tank trace in Lindsey and others [@lindsey2026] reads 61-68 degrees Celsius with multi-day dips, about 10 degrees cooler and less regular than A009 in 2026, and the loggers may not sit in the same place in the tank, so the 2025 and 2026 schedules cannot be compared directly. And the creek shows little sign of the resort cycle. The hourly conductance difference between SBGG and SBRR has a daily range of about 30 uS/cm, roughly 4 percent of the mean difference of about 740 uS/cm. Its mean daily shape resembles the tank's (r = 0.50 over the 24 hourly means on weekdays and 0.87 on weekends), but hour by hour over 73 overlapping days the correlation is only 0.07. A shared daily driver such as creek temperature or evapotranspiration cannot be excluded, so the resort is not shown to control the creek's conductance difference.

@fig-lindsey-loggers sets the logger traces read from Lindsey and others' Figure 3 (1-8 July 2025, digitized by eye to about 1 degree Celsius) beside A009 and A005 over an 8-day window in July 2026. The comparison is limited by sensor position and by the different years. A009 sits near 76 degrees Celsius with a swing under 3 degrees, while the 2025 tank trace has a median near 67 and dips to 61. Her main-fissure logger, shown as a daily mean of about 76 degrees Celsius (the trace itself swings about 2.5 degrees each day), is not known to be at the same point as A005 at SBF_0001, which ranged from 35 to 72 degrees Celsius with a median near 48 in the window shown, so the fissure difference should not be read as change through time. Her uncapped-well trace (89-90 degrees Celsius) has no counterpart in this project and is not plotted.

```{r fig-lindsey-loggers}
  alt = "Two panels, fissure and resort tank: 2025 traces from Lindsey and others against this project's 2026 loggers, which run warmer at the tank.",
  id = "fig-lindsey-loggers",
```

**What the thermal layer cannot show.** Lindsey and others tuned the imagery to ground-control
targets, but this project has not independently checked the exported TIFF against logger
data: no logger record overlaps the flight windows, and loggers sit in water or fumaroles
while the camera sees the surface skin. Where the TIFF has temperature data at a logger
site it reads far below the logger (the resort tank about 43 degrees Celsius, at the ramp's
cap, against 62-66 in July; SBS_0006 about 14 against 66), as expected for a surface
measurement with a 44 degree ceiling. The flight date of the TIFF is not recorded, the
polygons are the area of hot surface and not the area of discharge, and the ellipse and
circle annotations are an analyst's choices. The GeoPackage export carries the polygons and
the alias groupings (as points and as lines to the matched historical features) so that all
of this can be checked against the imagery in ArcGIS.

## A baseline chemical-evolution characterization of the flowpath

Everything in this subsection is read from the mixing, reaction-path, and
geothermometer runs already reported above: no new PHREEQC execution was
needed. The samples feeding every result here were all collected
within the same field season, so this is explicitly a **one-time, same-era
baseline characterization**: a demonstration that this modeling approach
can reconstruct mixing, chemical evolution, and feature-type connectivity
along a flowpath from a single snapshot of data, not an iterative
refinement project. Further precision (tighter end-members, a paired
uncertainty estimate for inverse modeling, resolving SBS_0001's own
unresolved tension) is explicitly deferred to the same-day synoptic
sampling round proposed in Chapter 5, not pursued further here.

This baseline does two things for the rest of the proposal. First, it
connects the fissure-specific geochemistry above directly to the
creek-scale conductivity proxy work in Chapter 4: both are, at bottom,
asking how far, and in what chemical form, the same thermal signal travels
from its source, and the mixing fractions below are the quantitative link
between the two. Second, it gives a chemical baseline for the Lower Sinter
Terrace as it stood in this field season: after the June 2025 eruption,
following the two-year buildup described in Chapter 1, and while the
terrace is still visibly changing, including the new hot spring the author
and Dave found in August 2026 and the growing sulfur deposit documented the
following month. Every new feature found at the terrace from here forward
can be checked against this same mixing/gain-loss framework to ask the same
question asked of SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 below: does it share the fissure's
deep chemical signature, and if so, does it behave more like a well or more
like a spring once that water nears the surface? That is a concrete,
repeatable test this baseline makes available for the ongoing spring and
well remapping, not just a one-off result.

**How much of each discharge point is fissure-strength fluid, and how does
that connect to the downstream proxy record?** Using the 
already-computed Cl-based mixing fraction against the fissure and SBRR
end-members, shown in @fig-mixingfraction, the three Low Sinter
Terrace springs and seep sit at 0.77-0.89 (mostly fissure-strength fluid,
diluted only modestly), the nearby well (SBW_0001) sits lower at 0.57, and
the resort tank exceeds the fissure reference itself (1.04, already
documented as a finding, not an error). SBRR itself anchors the dilute end
by definition; its downstream partner SBBV, several kilometers further down
Steamboat Creek, still implies about 14 percent fissure-strength fluid by
chloride alone: the same signal, at a much smaller concentration, that
the 58.7 liter per second thermal-discharge
estimate is built on. This is the direct link between the fissure-specific
chemistry above and the creek-scale conductivity proxy work: the same
conservative mixing framework explains both.

```{r fig-mixingfraction}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/mixing_fraction_by_target.png",
  "Real Cl-based mixing fraction (fraction fissure end-member) for every downgradient target, colored by feature type.",
  alt = "Horizontal bar chart of mixing fraction for six targets, sorted from SBBV (lowest) to the resort tank (highest, exceeding 1).",
  id = "fig-mixingfraction"
)
```

```{r tbl-mixingfraction}
mix_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/mixing_fraction_summary_table.csv")
knitr::kable(
  mix_tbl, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Target", "Feature type", "Mixing fraction (fissure end-member)"),
  caption = "Chloride-based conservative-mixing fraction against the fissure (f=1) and SBRR (f=0) end-members, for every downgradient target, sorted low to high."
)
```

**What is gained or lost, species by species, and does it distinguish
feature types?** Comparing each target's measured chemistry against
what the same Cl-based mixing fraction would predict if every species
traveled conservatively, shown in @fig-gainloss, sodium comes back
essentially conservative everywhere (within 6 percent), the direct
justification for treating chloride and sodium as reliable tracers in this
system. Potassium is modestly gained everywhere (13-31 percent), an open
signal plausibly reflecting mild clay or feldspar exchange, not chased
further here. Sulfate and alkalinity are where the feature-type
distinction shows up, sharpened in @fig-springswells: **every spring and
the seep gain far more sulfate relative to conservative mixing than either
well** (44-62 percent versus -3 to 20 percent), and alkalinity is **gained
at both wells but lost at two of the three springs**: opposite signs for
the same species, split cleanly along feature type. Plausible mechanisms
for both: open spring and seep discharge points are exposed to the
atmosphere in a way a cased well is not, so near-surface oxidation of
residual hydrogen sulfide to sulfate, and carbon dioxide degassing that
would otherwise support alkalinity, both have more opportunity to happen
before a sample is ever collected.

```{r fig-gainloss}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/species_gainloss_heatmap.png",
  "Measured concentration versus the conservative-mixing prediction for six species, for every downgradient target, expressed as percent gained or lost.",
  alt = "Tile plot with targets on rows and species on columns, colored and labeled by percent deviation from conservative mixing.",
  id = "fig-gainloss"
)
```

```{r fig-springswells}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/springs_vs_wells_residuals.png",
  "Sulfate and alkalinity gain/loss relative to conservative mixing, grouped by feature type, isolating the clearest feature-type pattern from the full heatmap above.",
  alt = "Two-panel bar chart, one panel for alkalinity and one for sulfate, bars colored by feature type (well, well resort, spring, seep).",
  id = "fig-springswells"
)
```

```{r tbl-gainloss}
gl_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/species_gainloss_summary_table.csv")
knitr::kable(
  gl_tbl, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Target", "Feature type", "Na", "SO4", "Si", "B", "K", "Alkalinity"),
  caption = "Real percent gain (+) or loss (-) relative to conservative mixing, by species and target, numeric companion to the heatmap above."
)
```

**How does the temperature record fit into this, and is this a
chemically feasible connection for every feature type, or not?** The
three-stage cooling picture in @fig-tempprofile (Na/K reservoir estimate,
quartz-equilibration estimate, measured discharge temperature) and the
Steamboat Creek re-warming between SBRR and SBBV are both drawn directly
from values already reported above, placed side by side here as the
clearest single summary figure for this subsection. Put all of this
together and the answer is neither a clean "yes, connected" nor a
clean "no, not connected": the Na/K reservoir-temperature agreement
(173-190 degrees Celsius across every thermal feature, not just the
three used for the formal agreement test above) is consistent with one
shared deep source feeding wells, springs, and the seep alike. But the
sulfate, alkalinity, and quartz versus measured temperature patterns above
show that **springs and wells diverge systematically in near-surface
process**, not randomly: springs and the seep show more cooling below their
own quartz-equilibration temperature and a consistent sulfate-gain/
alkalinity-loss signature that the wells do not share. The more precise and
more defensible statement, given this baseline snapshot, is that these
features are chemically consistent with a shared deep source but **not**
chemically consistent with identical near-surface pathways: a specific,
testable distinction between spring-type and well-type connectivity that a
simple proximity map alone (SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 sit only 109 meters apart
yet show two of the most different fit behaviors on this flowpath, already
noted above) cannot provide on its own.

```{r fig-tempprofile}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/temperature_flowpath_profile.png",
  "A. Three-stage cooling (Na/K reservoir estimate, quartz-equilibration estimate, measured discharge) for all six thermal features, colored by feature type. B. Steamboat Creek's measured temperature rise from SBRR to SBBV.",
  alt = "Two panels: temperature across three cooling stages for six features colored by type, and creek temperature rising downstream.",
  id = "fig-tempprofile"
)
```

**A still-changing system: new field observations from the terrace.** The
system has continued to change since the 2026 poster was presented. In
August 2026, the author and Dave found a new seep-fed hot spring
discharging among bedrock boulders at a location that had not been active
before, at a spot the two of us walk regularly; a nearby resident
separately confirmed this was new. We returned the following month to
photograph and GPS-log it (@fig-hotspring, all photos from September 27,
2026, within about 150 meters of each other at the terrace, times and
coordinates taken from camera EXIF data rather than our own notes). At the
same time we noted two other changes: a native-sulfur deposit
(@fig-sulfur) that has visibly grown and still looks fresh rather than
weathered, and a seep (@fig-seep) discharging from the alluvial cover
directly onto the underlying hard sinter bedrock, an example of the
alluvium to bedrock contact the spring and well remapping below is designed
to document systematically rather than just stumbling across. Taken
together, these three observations support the poster's own conclusion
(fluids are still redistributing within an existing shallow conduit system
rather than the terrace having settled into a new, static state) and they
are the direct reason the remapping and monitoring work proposed below
needs to happen now rather than later.

```{r fig-hotspring}
  id = "fig-hotspring"
```


This same seep location was also photographed on an earlier visit,
shown side by side with the September 27, 2026 photo above in
@fig-seep-compare. The two visits document the same bare,
white-crusted alluvium on sinter feature over time rather than two
separate points, giving an informal before and after view of
how this specific discharge point looks across repeat visits.

```{r fig-seep-compare}
#| results: asis
```

## Hydrochemical endmember characterization

Following Objectives 1 and 3 above, every water sample with complete
major-ion chemistry (157 samples as of this writing) is assigned to a
hydrochemical facies using unsupervised clustering, cross-checked by
principal component analysis and an independent statistical classification
method, and compared against PHREEQC's own fluid-type classification. The
thermal end-member's chemistry (specifically its chloride to boron,
sodium to chloride, lithium to chloride, and silica to chloride ratios) is
then tracked across the 1950s, 1990s, and present eras to test whether the
source fluid's composition, and separately its modeled equilibrium state,
have remained stable over more than seventy years.

**Hydrochemical facies recover known geochemistry.** Clustering every
sample with complete major-ion chemistry, independently cross-checked by
principal component analysis and a classification method, recovers a pure
sodium-chloride thermal cluster, a dilute background-water cluster, and an
intermediate mixed cluster, without being told each sample's site type in
advance: three independent statistical approaches converging on the same
chemical structure, as shown in @fig-facies.

```{r fig-facies}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/facies/facies_pca_biplot.png",
  "Principal-component biplot of major-ion chemistry, colored by persisted hydrochemical-facies cluster assignment.",
  alt = "Principal component biplot of major-ion chemistry, points colored by hydrochemical facies cluster, showing thermal, mixed, and background groups.",
  id = "fig-facies"
)
```

## Evaluating conductance as a conservative proxy for chloride

Following Objective 2, every process capable of altering either
chloride or conductance independently is evaluated explicitly rather
than assumed away:

| Process | Alters chloride? | Alters conductance? |
|---|---|---|
| Dilution with meteoric water | Yes | Yes |
| Calcite/dolomite precipitation | No | Yes |
| Thermal/meteoric mixing | Yes | Yes |
| Silica precipitation | No | Slight |
| Ion exchange (sodium-calcium) | No | Slight to moderate |
| Evaporative concentration | Yes (concentrates) | Yes (concentrates), but in a different proportion than dilution/mixing |

Where a process alters conductance without a matching change in
chloride, that is a direct, falsifiable reason the proxy relationship
could fail at a given site or season, and this failure mode is
stated directly rather than smoothed over. The same framework is
then applied to any
outlier the eventual chloride-conductance calibration produces
(Objective 4): a sample sitting off the fitted relationship is checked
against this same process list before being treated as measurement
error.


## Chloride-conductivity calibration

This is the thesis's core analytical task, and it is explicitly not
yet executable with the data on hand: no chloride sample
currently overlaps the period the conductivity loggers have been
running closely enough to serve as a calibration pair. Once
paired samples exist (see the sampling plan below), the calibration
itself will be developed as a statistical regression of chloride
concentration against specific conductance, fit separately by site
type (outlet, creek, monitoring well, spring) and compared against a
single global model to test whether one relationship can serve the
whole system or whether site-specific calibrations are required.
Reported uncertainty will include both the regression's own
confidence interval and, where repeat sampling allows, an estimate of
how much the relationship drifts across seasons.

**Candidate model forms, and why each one is in the comparison.** Three
functional forms are fit and compared, each included for a specific,
stated reason rather than just "trying everything":

- A **plain linear regression** of chloride against specific conductance
  (and, where it improves fit, temperature). This is the simplest possible
  form, and the one most directly comparable to how specific conductance
  has already been used as a chloride proxy in other geothermal rivers
  [@mccleskey2012; @mccleskey2016]. In symbols, $\text{Cl} = \beta_0 +
  \beta_1 \cdot SC + \beta_2 \cdot T + \varepsilon$, where $SC$ is specific
  conductance, $T$ is temperature (included only if it measurably improves
  fit), and $\varepsilon$ is the model's residual (unexplained) error.
- A **log-linear fit** (chloride log-transformed before fitting), since
  chloride is strictly positive and spans more than an order of magnitude
  across site types, from dilute background wells to the thermal
  end-member: a plain linear fit on the raw scale tends to be pulled around
  by the highest-concentration samples and can predict a nonsensical
  negative chloride value at the dilute end, which a log transform avoids.
- A **generalized additive model** (GAM, fit with the mgcv package for R,
  following @wood2017), which allows the chloride versus conductance curve
  to bend where the data demands it, rather than assuming in advance
  that the relationship is a straight line (or a straight line in log
  space). In plain terms, a GAM replaces the single slope $\beta_1$ above
  with a flexible smooth curve $f(SC)$, estimated directly from the data,
  while still penalizing against overfitting a wiggly, implausible curve
  to noise.

A **random-forest model** (fit with the ranger package for R, following
@breiman2001) is also fit as a nonparametric benchmark: not because it is
expected to be the reported calibration (a random forest is an average over
many decision trees and does not return a usable equation a future field
technician could apply by hand), but because it establishes an upper bound
on how much predictive skill a very flexible model can extract from the
same predictors, against which the three simpler, reportable forms above
are judged. If the random forest substantially outperforms all three, that
is itself informative: it would mean the true relationship has structure
(for example, a site-type-dependent threshold) none of the simpler forms
can capture, and the calibration would need to be revisited rather than
finalized as a single equation. This comparison is not being designed from
scratch: the comparison has already been built and tested in two independent
implementations of the linear, additive and random-forest fits, exercised so
far only on simulated data standing in for the paired samples that the
calibration window is designed to collect.

**Validation.** Chloride and conductance are both autocorrelated time
series (today's value is correlated with yesterday's), so ordinary random
k-fold cross-validation would leak information between adjacent, nearly
identical observations and overstate model skill. Every candidate model is
instead evaluated with rolling-origin (blocked, time-aware) cross-
validation, following the general time-series cross-validation guidance of
@bergmeir2012: each fold trains only on data up to a given point in time
and tests on data immediately after it, mirroring how the calibration would
actually be applied going forward (predicting ahead, never predicting a
date the model has already effectively "seen" through a neighboring
sample). This is implemented twice, once as a purpose-written routine and once with a
standard resampling package. Reported skill is the cross-validated
root mean square error (RMSE, the typical size of a prediction's error, in
the same units as chloride itself) and mean absolute error averaged across
folds, not a single in-sample fit statistic that would overstate how well
the model generalizes to a new, unseen sample.

**Choosing between a global and a site-specific model.** Because the
candidate forms above span different model families (linear, GAM, random
forest), and because a global model and a site-specific model are not
always nested within each other, the primary comparison is cross-validated
RMSE under the same rolling-origin scheme described above: the one
criterion that is valid across every model family and every candidate
grouping. Where two models are nested (for example, a linear or
GAM model with and without a site-type interaction term), Akaike
Information Criterion (AIC) and a likelihood-ratio test are reported as a
secondary check, since both are only meaningful for nested models fit by
maximum likelihood and would be misleading if applied across model
families. A site-specific model is adopted over the global model only if it
improves cross-validated RMSE by a margin larger than the fold to fold
variability in that RMSE, not from a marginal or single-fold improvement
alone.


## Minimum sampling-frequency design via Monte Carlo subsampling

This analysis directly serves RQ2 and has already been carried out, using
the densely sampled specific-conductance record as a stand-in for an
equally dense chloride record: since no such dense chloride record exists
yet, this tests how much information is lost by sampling a continuous
signal sparsely, in units of the conductance signal itself, not yet the
chloride calibration or the integrated mass flux it would ultimately feed.
The eventual quantity of interest is mass flux, the time integral of the
product of chloride concentration and discharge,

$$
F = \int C(t)\,Q(t)\,dt ,
$$

where $C(t)$ is chloride concentration and $Q(t)$ is discharge; the same
Monte Carlo procedure already computes a mass-flux percent
error whenever a paired discharge series is supplied, evaluated numerically
by trapezoidal integration, and is ready to report that number directly
once a discharge record is paired with the conductance record at the
same two sites: not done here, since the point of this specific run is to
characterize how well the concentration signal itself survives sparse
sampling, independent of discharge.

**The method, step by step.** For each candidate chemistry-sampling
interval: 1, 2, 3, 7, and 14 days:

1. Draw a random start offset within the first interval (for a 7-day
   interval, the first simulated "sample" might fall on day 2, day 5, or
   any other day of that first week).
2. Subsample the measured, dense conductance record at that fixed interval
   starting from the chosen offset; this mimics "what if a field
   campaign had only grabbed a sample every N days, starting on this
   particular day."
3. Linearly interpolate between just those sparse points to reconstruct an
   approximation of the full continuous record, exactly as if the sparse
   samples were all the information available.
4. Compare the reconstruction to the full-resolution record point by
   point (root mean square error, as a percent of the mean).
5. Repeat steps 1-4 two hundred times per candidate interval, each with a
   new random start day.

Step 5 is why this is a *Monte Carlo* exercise and not a single
calculation: which specific days a field campaign happens to land on
is arbitrary, and a schedule that happens to always catch a daily peak (or
always catch a trough) will look artificially better or worse than one that
samples more evenly through the cycle. Repeating with two hundred random
offsets characterizes that phase-dependent uncertainty directly, rather
than reporting one number that might just reflect a lucky or unlucky start
day: shown directly in @fig-mcspread, which plots the full spread of all
two hundred draws per interval rather than only their mean.

**The corrected result, with air-exposure days removed.** The analysis was
re-run against the conductance record after removing (1) the readings the QC
detector flagged as retrieval artifacts or spikes, (2) the three days before
each logger retrieval, because field notes show the loggers sat in open air
for at least several days before each pull, and (3) the SBGG record from
29 September 2026 onward, when SBGG began to be exposed to open air (its
logger temperature range rises from about 5 C to 7-8 C on that date, in line
with the field observation of late-September to early-October exposure). Those
readings are instrument artifacts, not signal, and including them would inflate
the reconstruction error in a way unrelated to the sampling-frequency question.
The three-day pre-retrieval window is a stated choice, because the air
exposure is not visible in conductivity itself; widening it to seven days and
moving the SBGG onset to 25 September or 2 October changes the mean error by
no more than about 0.6 percentage points (sensitivity runs archived with the analysis). With the exclusions, daily sampling gives a
mean reconstruction error of 3.6% of mean specific conductance at SBRR and
3.1% at SBGG; every other day sampling gives 4.3% and 4.1%; weekly sampling
6.9% and 7.8%; and biweekly sampling 9.5% and 8.5%. The degradation is smooth,
not a sharp cliff, so the choice of interval is a precision versus cost
trade-off rather than a hard threshold. The worst case, the 95th percentile
across the 200 simulated campaigns, widens faster than the mean: at SBRR it
rises from 4.0% (daily) to 4.8% (every other day), 7.7% (weekly) and 12.1%
(biweekly); at SBGG it is 5.0% for both daily and every other day sampling,
then 9.8% (weekly) and 13.2% (biweekly). Relaxing from daily to every other day
sampling therefore costs little in the typical case, while a weekly or
biweekly schedule could land well above the mean depending on which day the
campaign started. This is a quantitative basis for the sampling design below.

**What the chloride models have been run on so far: synthetic data.** The
Monte Carlo result above is the only quantity that has been computed on the
measured record, and it is the only analysis used to choose the sampling
frequency. The linear, GAM and random-forest chloride models have not been
fitted to measured paired samples, because no chloride sample yet overlaps the
logger record (zero pairs). They have been run only as a code test on a
simulated data set generated for that purpose: 60 samples every three days from 1 May 2026, with
$SC = 300 + 40\sin(2\pi d/365) + \mathrm{N}(0,15)$,
$T = 15 + 8\sin(2\pi (d-60)/365) + \mathrm{N}(0,1.5)$ and
$\mathrm{Cl} = 1 + 0.071\,SC_{lag} + 0.1\,T_{lag} + \mathrm{N}(0,1.5)$, where the
lag is six days. The slope 0.071 is taken from the single measured SBRR pair
(Cl 17.1 mg/L at 241 uS/cm, 2026-05-01), so the simulated chloride stays in a
realistic range; every other number is made up. Because the data were
generated from a known linear rule, the exercise shows only that the fitting
and cross-validation code runs and recovers a known relationship; it says
nothing about how well a GAM would perform on Steamboat Creek, and it did not
influence the choice of sampling interval. The same is true of the only
fit available, a linear regression on 181 historical NDEP pairs at Rhodes Road
(1987-2025; $R^2 = 0.65$), which predates the loggers. The calibration campaign
proposed below supplies the first pairs for the GAM.

**Proposed sampling design.** This proposal explicitly proposes a
chloride sampling campaign at the two existing conductivity-logger
stations, **SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) and SBGG (Geiger Grade,
downstream)**, because those are the only two points where a chloride
measurement can be directly paired against an already-running, continuous
conductance record. Because no chloride sample yet overlaps that
deployment, the highest-priority field task is a short, two to four week,
daily to sub-daily intensive sampling campaign at both SBRR and SBGG: and,
given that the loggers have already been running since mid-July 2026, there is
no reason to wait for a conventional spring/summer field season to start
it. This proposal now plans to begin that intensive window as soon as
possible (targeting this fall/winter), specifically so that monthly
follow-through sampling can begin right away rather than months from now.
Following the intensive window, chloride sampling should continue at
roughly monthly intervals at both SBRR and SBGG for a full annual cycle
(not just "the remainder of the year," but a complete
winter low flow to spring runoff to summer baseflow to fall transition
loop) with additional samples timed around large storms and
spring snowmelt, when the relationship is most likely to break down.
Starting earlier and running a full year of monthly pairs turns RQ1's
seasonal-stability question from a stated hypothesis into something this
proposal can actually test with data, rather than extrapolating from
the roughly twelve-week, summer to early fall conductance record the Monte Carlo
analysis above currently has to work with. Every calibration sample should
also carry major-ion chemistry, and a subset should carry
delta-18-O/delta-D isotopes, since chloride alone cannot distinguish simple
mixing from evaporative concentration. A conventional practical minimum of
15-20 paired samples would support a stable regression across the sampled
range; a full year of monthly sampling plus the intensive
daily to sub-daily window comfortably clears the more defensible 30-40-pair
target without relying on a single season's data. @tbl-samplingplan lays
out this same design as a single table: site, analyte set, frequency, and
the reasoning behind each row.

| Site | What is sampled | Frequency / timing | Why |
|------------------|----------------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) | Chloride, major ions (Na, K, Ca, Mg, SO4, alkalinity), field pH/temperature/specific conductance | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks (intensive window, starting fall/winter 2026) | Establishes the calibration's short-timescale behavior and its noise floor against the logger's own continuous record. |
| SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream) | Same analyte set as SBRR | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks, concurrent with the SBRR window | A second, independently calibrated site tests whether one relationship serves the whole system (RQ1) or whether SBRR and SBGG need their own equations. |
| SBRR and SBGG | Same analyte set as above | Monthly, for a full annual cycle following the intensive window | Tests seasonal stability (RQ1) across winter baseflow, spring runoff, summer baseflow, and fall transition, not just one season. |
| SBRR and SBGG (opportunistic) | Same analyte set as above | Additional unscheduled samples around large storms and spring snowmelt | These are the conditions most likely to break the conservative-mixing assumption (dilution, flashy runoff); oversampled rather than left to chance. |
| A prioritized subset of the above (SBRR and SBGG) | delta-18-O / delta-D isotopes | Roughly one isotope sample per season, timed with a regular chloride visit | Chloride alone cannot distinguish simple thermal/meteoric mixing from evaporative concentration (both raise chloride); isotopes can. |

: Proposed chloride sampling plan at the two conductivity-logger
stations. {#tbl-samplingplan}

**Sampling-frequency feasibility.** The Monte Carlo result described
in the Methods section above and shown in @fig-mc is itself a
completed preliminary analysis, not a planned one.

```{r fig-mc}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/sampling_frequency_error_curve.png",
  "Monte Carlo reconstruction-error curve for candidate chemistry-sampling intervals.",
  alt = "Line plot of Monte Carlo reconstruction error versus chemistry-sampling interval, from daily to biweekly sampling.",
  id = "fig-mc"
)
```

The line plot above shows only the *mean* RMSE across the 200 draws per
interval: it hides how much a single field campaign's result could
vary just from which day it happened to start on. Plotting the full
distribution of draws, shown in @fig-mcspread, makes that spread directly
visible: the boxes widen noticeably at longer intervals, and a
biweekly campaign could plausibly land anywhere from roughly 7% to 13%
reconstruction error depending purely on which day it started, while daily
and every other day sampling keep nearly every draw in a tight band near
the mean. This is the quantified reason the intensive
daily to sub-daily calibration window proposed above is recommended over a
coarser interval: not only is the *average* error lower, the *worst-case*
outcome from an unlucky start day is far less severe.

```{r fig-mcspread}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/sampling_frequency_spread_boxplot.png",
  "Spread across 200 Monte Carlo draws (random start-offset) for each candidate sampling interval, SBRR and SBGG.",
  alt = "Boxplot of reconstruction RMSE across 200 Monte Carlo draws, by candidate sampling interval and site, showing widening spread at longer intervals.",
  id = "fig-mcspread"
)
```

## Post-eruption chloride-flux monitoring

Following RQ4, the chloride mass-balance method is applied to every
date on which chloride and discharge are both available at the two gauging
stations, and the result is compared against the full historical record
(White's 1950s/1960s estimates, Sorey and Spielman's 2008-2016 values, and
the 2026 poster estimate) to ask whether outflow has measurably changed
since the eruption, while explicitly accounting for the seasonal
variability Sorey and Spielman themselves documented at these same sites.
The same conservative-ratio tracking used for endmember stability (above)
is applied here as a second, independent line of evidence: a stable ratio
across the eruption itself would support continuity of the same source
fluid, while a shift would support a change in fluid provenance or mixing
pathway.

**A database-grounded discharge estimate.** Applying the
chloride mass-balance method to the one date with paired
chloride and discharge measurements at both gauging stations gives
58.7 liters per second, a single-day value that sits within, not
clearly above or below, the broader 1955-2026 record (roughly
30-90 L/s depending on year and method) once Sorey and Spielman's own
documented seasonal variability is taken into account, shown in
@fig-discharge.

**A three-month field-parameter time series.** A roughly monthly
record of pH, temperature, and specific conductance across fourteen sites
(six injection-side ports and eight shallow monitoring and domestic wells)
spanning late September through December 2025 shows a stable, consistent
gap between the injection-side ports (pH 5.8-6.3) and the shallow well
network (pH 7.0-8.1), present in every round rather than as a single-date
artifact. Two individual wells also show opposite-direction
multi-month trends not explained by any change in the other monitored
parameter at the same well, a pattern that cautions against treating any
single field parameter as a universal proxy for thermal fraction across the
whole system.

## Uncertainty in the chloride-based discharge

The thermal inflow between SBRR and SBBV is computed as

$$
Q_{TW} = \frac{Q_{BV}\,C_{BV} - Q_{RR}\,C_{RR}}{C_{TW}},
$$

where $Q$ is stream discharge, $C$ is chloride concentration, the subscripts mark the downstream station (BV), the upstream station (RR) and the thermal end-member (TW), and the end-member concentration is 820 mg/L following Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992]. The uncertainty of $Q_{TW}$ follows from adding the relative errors of each term in quadrature. As planning values, and not measured errors, take 10 percent for each stream discharge, 5 percent for each laboratory chloride value and 3 percent for the end-member concentration. The two chloride fluxes on 1 May 2026 are then 53.5 g/s (SBBV) and 5.4 g/s (SBRR), each uncertain by about 11 percent; their difference, 48.1 g/s, is uncertain by about 6.0 g/s (12.5 percent), and with the end-member term the thermal inflow is 58.7 plus or minus about 7.6 L/s (13 percent). The upstream term is small, so the result is controlled by the downstream discharge and chloride. Three consequences follow. A change in thermal inflow smaller than about 15 percent cannot be separated from measurement error on a single date. The 1 May value and the poster's 27 L/s average differ by more than this error, but they are not the same quantity (one date against an average over several), so the comparison does not yet say that discharge changed. And the largest single improvement available is better discharge at SBBV, which is why the proposal asks for a flow measurement or a rated station at the downstream logger.

## The sampling plan in depth: calibration pairs, the Monte Carlo design, and Lower Terrace mapping

Sampling serves three purposes in this thesis, and the plan is built so that one visit serves all three: pairing chloride with conductance for the calibration (RQ1), setting how often chloride must be measured (RQ2), and characterizing the discharge points of the Lower Sinter Terrace so that the thermal map can be tied to chemistry (RQ3 and RQ4).

**What the Monte Carlo test establishes, and what it does not.** The test draws 200 random start days for each candidate interval, subsamples the conductance record at that interval, interpolates between the samples, and compares the reconstruction with the full record (the procedure is given above). @tbl-mcsummary gives the result with air-exposure days removed. Daily and every other day sampling reconstruct the record to within about 3-5 percent of its mean; weekly sampling to 7-8 percent, with a worst case near 10 percent; biweekly sampling to 9-10 percent, with a worst case of 12-13 percent. The test covers the concentration signal only, not mass flux, because no discharge record overlaps the loggers, and it is a statement about conductance, not chloride, until the calibration pairs exist. The daily swing in conductance is only 9-12 uS/cm at either station, so time of day matters little for the schedule. The test will be re-run on chloride once paired samples exist, and with discharge once a discharge series overlaps the loggers.

| Sampling interval | SBRR mean (%) | SBRR 95th percentile (%) | SBGG mean (%) | SBGG 95th percentile (%) |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Daily | 3.6 | 4.0 | 3.1 | 5.0 |
| Every other day | 4.3 | 4.8 | 4.1 | 5.0 |
| Weekly | 6.9 | 7.7 | 7.8 | 9.8 |
| Biweekly | 9.5 | 12.1 | 8.5 | 13.2 |

: Reconstruction error of the conductance record as a percent of its mean, over 200 random campaigns per interval, with air-exposure days removed. {#tbl-mcsummary}

**Calibration pairs.** The design is an intensive daily to sub-daily window followed by monthly sampling across a full annual cycle (@tbl-samplingplan). A reasoned minimum is 15-20 pairs for a stable regression and 30-40 for a seasonally defensible one, and a tier of about 40 analyses is recommended for a one-person thesis. This is a reasoned count, not a power analysis, because no chloride-conductance pairs exist yet to compute one against. Pairing chloride with the major ions lets the mixing model be checked in the same samples, and about one isotope sample per season at the two creek stations is the only way to separate evaporation from conservative mixing.

**Mapping the Lower Terrace.** @tbl-lstsampling lists proposed sampling by source, with the sources taken from the thermal map. The counts are a starting point to be fitted to the laboratory budget and to site access, and they come in addition to the roughly 40 calibration analyses.

| Source (from the thermal map) | Why | Proposed samples per year | Measurements |
|-------------------|-----------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| Fissure zone (SBF_0001, SBF_0002, NV26-1) | Deep-source end-member; gas repeat | 4 water (quarterly), 2 gas | Major ions, boron, lithium, silica, 2 isotope samples; gas composition |
| Lower Terrace channel (largest anomaly, 161 m^2^) | Whether it shares the fissure's source | 4 (quarterly), access permitting | Major ions, silica, field temperature, pH, conductance |
| Creek-corridor springs and seeps (17 polygons; SBS_0001, SBS_0002, SBS_0006; springs 45, 46, 44e and 50n by alias) | Diffuse thermal inflow to the creek | 12 (6 springs, 2 seasons) | Chloride, major ions, field parameters |
| Resort tank and overflow, with the creek above and below the entry point | Resort share of the thermal inflow | 12 (4 dates, 3 points) | Chloride, conductance, temperature, flow |
| Capped eruption pipe (SBW_0003), if accessible | The 2025 eruption pipe | 2 | Major ions, temperature, water level |

: Proposed Lower Terrace sampling by source, in addition to the calibration analyses. {#tbl-lstsampling}

**Repeat thermal surveys.** The 488 m^2^ at or above 30 degrees Celsius is a baseline. If NBMG can repeat the calibrated drone flights each season, the same pixel to polygon method gives a change metric (area by source and season) at no laboratory cost, and a repeat of the October 2025 flight would show whether the creek-corridor springs and the fissure zone are growing, shrinking or moving.

**Decision rules.** After the first full cycle, residuals are compared by season and site type. A single calibration is kept only if its error is acceptable against a threshold set explicitly with the committee (no default threshold is assumed); otherwise site-specific equations are reported with their uncertainty, as RQ1's deliverable states.

## Proposed extension: a Leapfrog geologic model to inform mixing pathways and reaction paths

Rachel Micander's proposal builds a 3-D structural model in Leapfrog and ArcGIS from well collars, directional surveys, mud logs, well chips, borehole-image logs and geophysical products, to show fluid pathways, structure and the distribution of sinter and other rock below the surface. This proposal borrows that workflow at a smaller scope and for a different purpose. The model is not meant to explain structure or to simulate flow. It gives the chemistry a geometry.

**What the model would do.** It has four jobs. First, compartments: grouping samples by lithology and fault block, so that end-members and mixing pairs are chosen within and across compartments on stated geologic grounds. Second, pathways: giving path lengths and orientations for the 1-D mixing models along the fissure to creek flowpath, so that mixing fraction can be plotted against distance. Third, reaction paths: showing which rock the water meets (altered alluvium, volcanics, altered granodiorite, sinter), so that the phases supplied to the PHREEQC reaction-path titration are chosen from the geology and not by trial; the calcium-alkalinity tension at SBS_0001, which no simple phase set resolved, is the open question this targets. Fourth, a check on the chemistry: comparing the principal components of the PHREEQC output by compartment.

**Data on hand.** Collars, depths and elevations for 110 wells (elevations from the 1 m DEM unless a permit or survey value exists); 140 lithology intervals from the NBMG permit compilation and 158 from the 27 well logs in Collar's thesis (86 linked to wells); Skalbeck's cross-sections and 241 point depths to the units Qal, Tv, AltKgdpKm and Kgd; 9 faults, 53 fissure traces and the sinter-terrace outline; and the thermal polygons. All are exported in UTM zone 11N with Z from the DEM. The limits are that every hole is treated as vertical except 83C-6ST1, which has a deviation survey, that lithology quality varies, and that no permeability data exist.

**Workflow.** The database is exported to Leapfrog (fault network, lithologic units, intersections with the wells); compartment labels are written back to the database; the PHREEQC and mixing runs are grouped by compartment; the principal-component analysis is repeated by compartment. The fault traces digitized in ArcGIS are the main dependency, and nine are on file.

**A principal-component analysis of the PHREEQC output.** @fig-phreeqc-pca shows a first version: 381 samples and 17 variables (log activities of the major ions, saturation indices of calcite, aragonite, dolomite, gypsum, anhydrite, halite, quartz and chalcedony, pH and ionic strength). The first component, 49.5 percent of the variance, is salinity: ionic strength, sodium, chloride, sulfate and the halite and gypsum saturation indices. It separates the creek waters from the thermal-influenced wells and outlets. The second, 28.1 percent, is pH and carbonate saturation. The analysis will be repeated with the Leapfrog compartment as the grouping variable and on the terrace flowpath alone.

```{r fig-phreeqc-pca}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/phreeqc_pca.png",
```

## Resistivity, collaborators, and data access

**Resistivity.** Christopher Kratt (UNR geophysicist) may be able to run electrical-resistivity lines across the fissure zone, the terrace and the creek if the property owners give permission. Resistivity would add what chemistry and logs cannot: the extent of a conductive, clay-altered cap, the depth of the fissure zone, and the lateral extent of saline water between wells, which would give the Leapfrog model fault and cap geometry in the gaps. White and others carried out resistivity surveys at Steamboat in the 1960s [@white1964b], so the method has precedent at this site. Two lines are proposed as a first step: one across the fissure zone and the Low Terrace Fault, and one along the creek corridor through the resort. Whether this happens depends on access, equipment and schedule, so it is not a deliverable of this proposal.

**Historical Lower Terrace information and logs.** Phil Busick and Gene Savoy hold much of the history of the Lower Sinter Terrace properties. The requests to them are: records and any drilling or construction information for the capped eruption pipe (ten candidate identities are on file); well logs and permits for the resort and spa wells, including NDWR log 26097; water-right and pumping information for the resort well; their observations of when springs and fissures changed; and access for sampling, for a field measurement of the capped pipe, for a walk of the resort overflow, and for any geophysics. Rachel Micander and NBMG hold the 2022-2025 timeline and field observations.

**Ormat.** Following the list in Rachel Micander's proposal (well collars, directional surveys, mud logs, borehole-image logs and geophysical products), a request to Ormat would be limited to what bears on the Lower Terrace: Lower Steamboat production and injection well logs, water levels and pressures. Any release would need an agreement, and nothing in this proposal depends on it.

**Public records.** NDEP (UIC permits, U230 field forms and chemistry; a request for deeper-well water levels is pending), NDOM (permitted-well records) and NDWR (well logs; the resort's water-right records have not yet been retrieved).

## Geologic and hydraulic context: explicitly out of scope beyond what already exists

Beyond the bounded Leapfrog model proposed above, three further steps would eventually let this project's chemistry be tested
against subsurface structure and flow paths, rather than inferred
from chemistry and proximity alone: a digitized fault geometry, a full
three-dimensional Leapfrog geologic model built on top of it, and a MODFLOW
groundwater-flow model built on top of that. None of the three is pursued
as an active deliverable of this thesis, for the same reason in each case:
each needs an input this project does not yet have, and building any of
them without that input would produce a model dominated by untested
assumptions rather than constraints, exactly the outcome the batch-modeling
framing above is meant to avoid, not just defer elsewhere. Digitized fault
traces need a committed ArcGIS georeferencing session against the
fracture and air-photo-lineament map in Collar's thesis (Plate 3 and Figure 14 [@collar1990thesis]; a shorter version is in Collar and Huntley [@collar1990])
(chosen because it also shows selected wells and hot springs, several already resolved in this
database, giving natural control points; his Plate 1 (springs) and Plate 4 (stream stations) are the matching targets for tying White's spring numbers and his gaging stations to present locations); a calibrated hydraulic-
conductivity and storage-coefficient field needs pump-test drawdown
data, which does not yet exist for any Lower Sinter Terrace well (an
Aqtesolv analysis of such data, once collected, is a near-term
opportunity given the author's own ongoing groundwater hydrology
coursework, but is not assumed here on any fixed timeline). The only 
site-area transmissivity/storage-coefficient values on file today are
literature reference points, not a calibrated field: four dated aquifer
tests summarized by Sorey and Colvard [-@sorey1992] (roughly 1,250-9,500
square feet per day) and the thesis values of Collar [-@collar1990thesis]: 2,950-9,500 square feet per day from well and spring response, with a storage coefficient of 2.6e-3 (spring 42w, about
3,000 square feet per day, also in Collar and Huntley [-@collar1990]).

What already exists and is usable today, at essentially no
further cost, is worth naming so it is not lost alongside what is being
deferred: well collar, total-depth, and
completion-interval data for roughly half the wells on file, already
exported in Leapfrog's own input format and standing ready the moment
fault geometry exists to build on top of it; and a standing NDEP data
request for deeper-well water levels that would, if it comes through,
support a field-specific potentiometric surface (today, only two or
three wells inside the Steamboat field itself carry continuous, current
water-level data). Both are named here as next steps for whoever
picks this thread up next (the author included, time permitting) not as
deliverables of this proposal.

## Planned figures, not yet produced

Three figures central to the finished thesis cannot be produced yet,
and are described here rather than filled with a placeholder or an
unrepresentative result.

**A chloride-conductivity calibration plot** (chloride
concentration versus specific conductance, with a fitted regression
line and confidence band, by site type) will be the thesis's central
figure. It requires the paired chloride and conductance samples the
sampling plan above is designed to collect, and cannot be produced from
the current, unpaired records.

**A monitoring-network map over mapped structure and lithology** is the one map
that is not yet built. The thermal-infrared overlay it was once grouped with now exists
(@fig-map-fissure and @fig-map-resort, built from the georeferenced thermal map, the 53
mapped fissures, the 9 mapped faults and the project's own points), and the fault and
fissure traces are in the database. What the monitoring-network map still lacks is
subsurface lithology for most wells; it is a bounded GIS task once that exists, not an
open-ended modeling effort.

**A final conceptual model** of the Lower Sinter Terrace system,
synthesizing the chemical, discharge, and geologic evidence into a single
interpretive diagram, will be developed once the calibration and
tracer-ratio results above are complete: it is not sketched in
advance of that evidence.

**The three September 27, 2026 field photographs** above (@fig-hotspring,
@fig-sulfur, @fig-seep) carry GPS coordinates and timestamps in their
own camera EXIF data, confirmed directly rather than assumed, but have not
yet been run through this project's formal photo-location workflow
to become dated, located records in the underlying
database: that cataloguing step, not the figures themselves, is the remaining
task. The earlier-visit photo of this same seep used in @fig-seep-compare
and the SBGG installation photo in @fig-sbgg-install are field images
from this project's own work but, unlike the three September 27 photos,
their EXIF metadata no longer carries a capture date or GPS fix (confirmed
directly via exiftool, not assumed): both await the same cataloguing step once a coordinate and date are recovered or re-recorded.

# Preliminary schedule

The schedule below moves the intensive calibration window up to this
fall/winter (rather than a conventional spring field-season start) and
stretches monthly chloride sampling across a full annual cycle, so the
calibration can be tested against all four seasons before it is
treated as final, consistent with the sampling-design reasoning above.
Target dates are a planning structure, not fixed commitments, and will
be adjusted against the academic calendar and committee
availability as the work proceeds. The most direct risk to this
schedule is weather- or access-limited fieldwork during the
fall/winter calibration window; the contingency is the same full-year
monthly cadence shifted later into spring/summer 2027, at the cost of
testing fewer distinct seasons before the calibration is finalized.
A second risk is that the chloride-conductance relationship
turns out to be too noisy or site-specific to support a single
practical calibration; the contingency there is reported directly in
RQ1's own deliverable above (site-specific equations with stated
uncertainty, not a forced single model) rather than treated as a
schedule failure.

@fig-schedule sets the plan against what is already on file. The long records (weather and pressure from 1938, chemistry from 1950, water levels from 1952) are the historical frame; the continuous logger records are short, which is the reason the calibration window starts now and not in a later field season. # Expected products

- A calibration equation relating chloride to specific conductance, or a set of site-specific equations, with stated uncertainty.
- A quantitative recommendation for the minimum sampling frequency needed for ongoing chloride monitoring at Steamboat.
- A PHREEQC-based physical justification (or documented limitation) for using specific conductance as a chloride proxy at this site.
- An updated interpretation of thermal-water discharge and conservative-tracer behavior before and after the 2025 eruption.
- Two candidate manuscripts: *Conductivity-Based Monitoring of Chloride Discharge at Steamboat Hills* (targeting *Geothermics* or *Geothermal Energy*), and *Hydrochemical Evolution of the Lower Sinter Terrace System Following the 2025 Eruption* (drawing on the PHREEQC, tracer-ratio and historical-comparison results above).
- A three-dimensional conceptual geologic framework for the monitored wells and springs, explicitly scoped as context rather than a flow model.
- A source by source map of surface heat and a resort-share estimate for the Lower Sinter Terrace, and a bounded Leapfrog compartment model used to group the chemistry.

# Conclusion

After the June 2025 eruption, the plain question at Steamboat is whether the system has a new source or an old one with a new outlet. Sorey asked a version of it after the spring decline of the 1980s, and the 2026 poster written with Cary Lindsey asked it again from a handful of samples [@irvinlindsey2026]. The evidence there points to an old conduit reactivating, but it was gathered at poster speed. This proposal replaces that handful of samples with a method that can be repeated and whose uncertainty is stated.

The work will deliver three things. The first is a tested relation between specific conductance and chloride at two creek stations, with an error bound and a sampling interval no coarser than the data allow. If it holds across seasons, a logger that costs little to run can supply most of the record that has so far had to be assembled from sparse chloride samples, and the thermal discharge of Steamboat Creek stops being a once in several years estimate. The second is a source by source account of the Lower Sinter Terrace: where heat reaches the surface (488 m^2^ at or above 30 degrees Celsius), which discharge points share the fissure's fluid, how much of the creek's thermal inflow is pumped from the resort well, and how the water changes chemically between the fissure and the creek. The third is a modest geologic frame, built from the wells, logs, faults and fissures already on file, that lets samples be grouped by what they have flowed through and lets the choice of reactions in the geochemical models rest on the rock.

These results matter for different reasons to different readers. For the science, the 2025 eruption is the first event at Steamboat whose aftermath can be followed at this resolution, in a system with a 70-year discharge record to compare against, and a chloride-conductance proxy that works in thermal outflow would be useful at other geothermal systems where outflow is monitored by sampling. For regulators and operators, a calibrated proxy and a defensible sampling interval are a cheaper way to watch outflow than the current campaigns. For the owners of the Lower Terrace properties, the maps and the source attribution document what is changing and where.

The thesis does not claim to explain the cause of the reactivation. Whether changes in injection, regional groundwater, or the natural behavior of the conduit system were responsible needs operator data that this project does not hold, and the proposal says so where it matters. It does not build a flow model, and the thermal map, with its 44 degree ceiling and unrecorded flight date, supports attribution and area estimates rather than a heat budget. Each of these limits has a stated next step.

What holds the pieces together is that they are built to check one another. Chemistry, gas, thermal imaging, hydrology and time-series statistics share one database and one set of documented calculations, so that a conclusion reached one way, such as the gas geothermometer's reservoir temperature, can be tested against another, such as the water geothermometers or the chloride-based discharge. If the calibration holds, the same linkage lets each of those checks run continuously against a cheap sensor, and a one-time snapshot of Steamboat becomes a monitoring framework that whoever manages the system next can reuse.
